question: what's the most pell grant money you can get for 2026-27?
answer: For the 2026-27 award year, the maximum Federal Pell Grant is $7,395 and the minimum is $740. The Department set the maximum under continuing appropriations and said it could change, so check your aid offer or StudentAid.gov for the final figure. Most students don't get the maximum: your actual Pell depends on your SAI, your school's cost of attendance and how many credits you take.

sources.title: (GEN-26-01) 2026-27 Federal Pell Grant Maximum and Minimum Award Amounts

question: Who can actually get a Pell Grant?
answer: Pell Grants are for undergraduate students with financial need, and you apply by filing the FAFSA. You generally can't get one if you've already earned a bachelor's degree, and anyone with a graduate or professional degree is ineligible. There are narrow exceptions, such as certain postbaccalaureate teacher certification programs and the new short-term workforce programs. Your school's financial aid office decides your eligibility from your FAFSA results.

question: I already have a bachelor's in business. Can I get Pell to go back for a second bachelor's in nursing?
answer: Generally no. Once you've earned a bachelor's degree, you can't receive a Pell Grant for another undergraduate degree. The main exceptions are a very limited postbaccalaureate teacher certification provision and Pell-eligible short-term workforce programs, which bachelor's degree holders can use. You may still qualify for federal loans, so ask your school's financial aid office what's available for a second degree.

question: Can grad students get a Pell Grant?
answer: No. Pell Grants are only for students in an undergraduate course of study, and anyone who has earned a graduate or professional degree is ineligible. Graduate students may be able to get other aid, such as a TEACH Grant for an eligible master's program in teaching or federal loans. Your graduate school's financial aid office can tell you which programs apply to you.

question: How do they figure out how much Pell I get?
answer: Your school starts with your Scheduled Award, which is the most you could get for the year as a full-time, full-year student. For most students it's the maximum Pell minus your SAI, rounded to the nearest $5 and capped at your school's cost of attendance. The school then adjusts it for your enrollment intensity, so taking fewer credits means a smaller payment each term. Your aid offer shows the result, and the aid office can walk you through it.

question: my parents don't make much money. is there an automatic max pell thing?
answer: Yes, there's a path to the maximum Pell based on income. A dependent student qualifies if their parents aren't required to file a federal tax return, or if the parents' AGI is above zero and at or below 225% of the federal poverty guideline for a single parent, or 175% for parents who aren't single. Independent students qualify the same way using their own (and a spouse's) income. The FAFSA applies these tests for you, and your school confirms the result.

question: My SAI is 0. Does that mean I'm getting the full Pell?
answer: An SAI of 0 usually means your Scheduled Award is the maximum, because the calculated Pell is the maximum minus your SAI. What you actually receive can still be less: it's capped at your school's cost of attendance and reduced if you enroll less than full time. Your financial aid office makes the final calculation and shows it in your aid offer.

question: I go to a really cheap community college. Could my Pell be less than the max just because tuition is low?
answer: It can be. A Pell Grant can't be more than your Pell cost of attendance, so at a very low-cost school the award may be capped below the maximum. Cost of attendance isn't just tuition, though: it includes components like books, housing and food, and transportation, always based on a full-time student for a full year. Ask your financial aid office for the cost of attendance it used.

question: If I get a scholarship from my church, will my school cut my Pell Grant?
answer: A correctly calculated Pell Grant isn't reduced because you get other aid, with one exception. Starting in 2026-27, if your non-federal grants and scholarships together equal or exceed your cost of attendance, you can't receive Pell for that award year. Outside scholarships can still reduce other parts of your package, like loans or school grants, if your total aid would go over your need. Report any outside scholarship to your financial aid office so it can adjust your package correctly.

question: If I only take 9 credits instead of 12, how much of my Pell do I get?
answer: Pell is based on enrollment intensity, which is your credits divided by your school's full-time standard (at least 12 credits for undergraduates). At a school where 12 credits is full time, 9 credits is 75% intensity and 6 credits is 50%, and your Pell for that term is reduced to match. Your school's full-time standard and its calculation decide the exact number, so check with the aid office before you change your schedule.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 3: Pell Grant Enrollment Intensity and Cost of Attendance

question: Can part-time students even get Pell?
answer: Yes. Part-time students can receive Pell Grants, and the award is prorated for how much you're enrolled. Schools don't have discretion to refuse to pay an otherwise eligible part-time student, including in summer or intersession terms. Your financial aid office will calculate the reduced amount based on your enrollment each term.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 3: Pell Grant Enrollment Intensity and Cost of Attendance

question: im only taking one class this semester. do i still get any pell?
answer: You can still be eligible if you're enrolled less than half time, but the award is often much smaller. For less-than-half-time students, only certain cost-of-attendance components count, so things like personal expenses are left out and housing and food are limited. Because a Pell Grant can't exceed your cost of attendance, that lower budget can cap your award. Your financial aid office can tell you what you'd receive for one class.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 3: Pell Grant Enrollment Intensity and Cost of Attendance

question: I want to drop a class early in the term. Will that change my Pell?
answer: It can. If you drop before you've started attending all your classes, your school must recalculate your Pell for that term using your lower enrollment. After you've attended all your classes, recalculation depends on the school's written policy. Being charged for a dropped class doesn't stop a required recalculation, so talk to your financial aid office before you drop.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 7: Initial Calculations, Recalculations, and Overawards

question: Can I use Pell for summer classes if I already used my Pell in fall and spring?
answer: Possibly, through what's called Year-Round Pell. You may be able to receive up to 150% of your Scheduled Award in an award year, which can pay for a summer term after fall and spring. To receive these additional funds you must be enrolled at least half time in that payment period, and you still have to meet the usual lifetime limits. Ask your school's financial aid office whether you qualify and how it handles summer.

question: Is there a limit on how long I can get Pell?
answer: Yes. There's a lifetime limit called Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU), and you can't receive more Pell once you reach 600%. Each Scheduled Award (one year of full-time Pell) counts as 100%, so the limit is six Scheduled Awards, roughly six years or 12 semesters of full-time enrollment. Part-time awards use up less of it. Your financial aid office can tell you how much you've used.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)
34 CFR Part 690: Federal Pell Grant Program (eCFR)

question: Does going part-time use up my Pell lifetime eligibility slower?
answer: Yes. LEU counts the percentage of a full Scheduled Award you actually receive, not the number of terms you attend. A term at half-time enrollment uses less of your lifetime limit than a full-time term, so a part-time student can receive Pell over more terms. The total can never pass six Scheduled Awards.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: Where can I see how much of my lifetime Pell I've used?
answer: Your Pell lifetime eligibility used appears in your federal aid records, and the handbook lists the FAFSA Submission Summary among the places it's reported. Your school can also see your current LEU through the Department's systems. If you're close to the limit, ask your financial aid office to confirm your exact percentage, since it's tracked to three decimal places.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: I'm close to running out of Pell eligibility. Do I just get nothing next year?
answer: Not necessarily. If you have some eligibility left, your school pays the remaining percentage of your Scheduled Award instead of a full award. For example, a student who has used 533% has 67% of a Scheduled Award left. Once you reach the 600% limit, no more Pell can be paid. Ask your aid office to calculate what you have left.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: My school closed before I finished. Did I lose the Pell I used there?
answer: You may be able to get that Pell eligibility restored. Students who received Pell at a school that closed, didn't complete their program and meet the timing rules can have the related lifetime eligibility restored, and restoration also applies with certain loan discharges like false certification, identity theft and borrower defense. Generally the student doesn't have to take action, because the Department flags eligible cases to schools. If you think you qualify, ask your new school's aid office to check.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: I got Pell years ago before I dropped out. Does that old Pell count against me now?
answer: Yes. The lifetime limit includes all Pell Grants you've ever received, going back to the program's start. Any earlier award reduces what you have left under the six-Scheduled-Award limit. Ask your financial aid office how much eligibility you still have.

sources.title: 2026-27 FSA Handbook, Vol. 7, Ch. 8: Pell Grant Lifetime Eligibility Used (LEU)

question: Is it true there's now an SAI cutoff for Pell? What is it for 2026-27?
answer: Yes. Starting with the 2026-27 award year, Public Law 119-21 makes a student ineligible for Pell if their SAI is equal to or greater than twice the maximum Pell Grant. For 2026-27 that threshold is an SAI of $14,790. The rule doesn't apply to students who qualify under the Special Rule for dependents of certain deceased servicemembers and public safety officers. Your school applies the rule using your FAFSA record.

question: Our income is low enough for minimum Pell but my SAI came out around 15,000. Can I still get some Pell?
answer: Under the 2026-27 rule, probably not. Public Law 119-21 makes any applicant with an SAI equal to or greater than twice the maximum Pell ineligible, and for 2026-27 that threshold is $14,790. This limit applies even to students who would otherwise meet the minimum Pell income tests, unless they qualify under the Special Rule for children of certain deceased servicemembers and public safety officers. If your SAI seems wrong, ask your financial aid office to review your FAFSA.

question: My dad works overseas and excludes his foreign income on taxes. Does that affect my Pell?
answer: It can. Starting with 2026-27, the foreign earned income exclusion reported on the FAFSA is added to AGI when the Department decides whether you qualify for the maximum or minimum Pell Grant. It isn't added for the SAI formula itself, where AGI still means the tax return figure and the exclusion is counted as untaxed income. Report the exclusion accurately on the FAFSA, and ask your financial aid office if you think it was handled incorrectly.

question: I got a full-ride scholarship that covers everything. Do I still get my Pell Grant on top?
answer: Not starting in 2026-27. Under Public Law 119-21, effective July 1, 2026, you can't receive a Pell Grant for an award year in which your non-federal grants and scholarships equal or exceed your cost of attendance. If your school learns of this before your final Pell disbursement, it must either reduce the non-federal aid below your cost of attendance, where it controls that aid, or return your Pell and cancel future disbursements. You keep Pell eligibility for later years if you have lifetime eligibility left, so talk to your aid office about your package.

answer: The rule looks at non-federal grant and scholarship aid, meaning aid from states, schools and private sources, that equals or exceeds your cost of attendance for the 2026-27 award year. Federal aid and loans aren't part of that test, and emergency grants don't count toward it. Students who get the maximum Pell under the Special Rule for children of certain deceased servicemembers or public safety officers are exempt. Your financial aid office decides how your specific awards are treated.

question: what is workforce pell and when does it start?
answer: Workforce Pell lets students use a Pell Grant for short, job-focused programs that used to be too short to qualify. It was created by Public Law 119-21 and starts July 1, 2026. An eligible program must run at least 8 weeks but less than 15 weeks and be at least 150 but fewer than 600 clock hours, or the credit-hour equivalent. Ask the school whether a specific program has been approved.

question: Which short-term programs actually qualify for Workforce Pell?
answer: A program qualifies only if the state's Governor and the Department approve it as an eligible workforce program. It must prepare students for high-skill, high-wage or in-demand jobs, meet employers' hiring requirements, and award academic credit toward a certificate or degree at the same school. For 2026-27 it also needs a completion rate and a job placement rate of at least 70 percent, and later its tuition will be tested against graduates' earnings. Correspondence, study-abroad and direct assessment programs don't qualify.

question: I already have a bachelor's degree. Can I use Workforce Pell for a short certificate program?
answer: Yes, potentially. Students who already have a bachelor's degree may receive Pell for an eligible workforce program, as long as they meet the other Pell requirements. You can't use it if you've earned a graduate credential or are enrolled or accepted into a program that leads to one. Your school's financial aid office determines whether you qualify.

question: Can I take out student loans for a Workforce Pell program too?
answer: No. Students in eligible workforce programs can receive only Pell Grants, not other federal student aid such as Direct Loans or work-study. You also can't receive Pell for two different workforce programs at the same time. Ask the school how it expects students to cover any costs Pell doesn't.

question: How do I apply for Workforce Pell? I don't see a box for it on the FAFSA.
answer: You still file the FAFSA, but there's no question asking whether you'll enroll in a workforce program. Your school's financial aid administrator determines that you're enrolled in an eligible workforce program and marks it on your record. Before you enroll, ask the school to confirm that the specific program has been approved for Workforce Pell.

question: Does Workforce Pell use up my lifetime Pell eligibility?
answer: It's still a Pell Grant: schools report Workforce Pell awards as Pell awards, and students must meet all the usual Pell requirements, including the lifetime eligibility limit. That means you need remaining lifetime eligibility to receive it. Exactly how much a short program counts against your limit depends on the award calculation, which is new and still being implemented, so confirm with your financial aid office.

question: What's FSEOG and how much is it?
answer: The Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant (FSEOG) is a grant for undergraduates with exceptional financial need who don't already have a bachelor's degree. For 2026-27 the award is at least $100 and usually no more than $4,000 for a full academic year, and up to $4,400 for an approved study-abroad program. Schools award it from a limited yearly allocation, so ask your financial aid office whether you can be considered.

question: I got Pell but no FSEOG. My friend got both. Why?
answer: FSEOG is a campus-based program, which means your school gets a limited amount of money each year and awards it until it runs out. Students with the lowest SAIs who are also getting Pell have first consideration, so even Pell recipients may not all receive it. Whether you get it depends on your SAI compared with other students and how much funding is left when your aid is packaged. Filing your FAFSA early and asking your aid office is your best move.

question: Can I get FSEOG in grad school?
answer: No. FSEOG is only for students enrolled as undergraduates who don't already have a bachelor's or first professional degree. Graduate students should ask their school's financial aid office about other options, such as federal loans or a TEACH Grant for an eligible teaching program.

question: What is a TEACH Grant?
answer: A TEACH Grant is for students in a TEACH Grant-eligible program who plan to teach in a high-need field at a school that serves low-income students. The full-time Scheduled Award for 2026-27 is $4,000, though a federal budget reduction (sequestration) lowers what students actually receive. In exchange, you must agree to teach full time for at least four years within eight years after you leave the program. If you don't, the grants turn into a loan you repay with interest.

question: what happens if i get a teach grant and then decide not to be a teacher?
answer: If you don't complete the teaching service, all the TEACH Grants you received convert to Direct Unsubsidized Loans that you must repay in full. Interest is charged from the date of each grant disbursement, not from the date it converts, so the balance can be larger than the grants. If you know you won't teach, you can ask to have them converted sooner to stop more interest from building up. Conversion counseling is available on StudentAid.gov.

question: Do I need good grades for a TEACH Grant, and is it based on need?
answer: There's an academic requirement but no financial need test. You generally need a cumulative GPA of at least 3.25 on a 4.0 scale, or a score above the 75th percentile on at least one section of a nationally normed admissions test. Current or former teachers and retirees getting a master's degree through an eligible program are exempt from that standard. TEACH isn't need-based, so your SAI doesn't determine eligibility.

question: What do I have to do before I get my TEACH Grant money?
answer: Before your first disbursement each award year, you complete TEACH Grant counseling and then sign an Agreement to Serve or Repay, both on StudentAid.gov. You have to sign a new agreement every award year you receive the grant. You'll also complete exit counseling before you leave your school. Your financial aid office can tell you its own deadlines.

question: How much TEACH Grant money can I get in total?
answer: For undergraduate and postbaccalaureate study combined, the limit is four Scheduled Awards, or $16,000. For an eligible master's program, the limit is two Scheduled Awards, or $8,000. Annual amounts are smaller if you enroll less than full time, and the amount actually paid is further lowered by sequestration. Your school will show the exact amount in your aid offer.

question: Is the Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant still a thing?
answer: Not as a separate grant for new recipients. That support now comes through the Pell Grant Special Rule, which lets an eligible student whose parent or guardian died in the line of duty receive the maximum Pell Grant regardless of their calculated SAI. Students who got Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant or Children of Fallen Heroes funds under the older guidance may keep that legacy status if they receive at least one disbursement every award year. Your school confirms eligibility with documentation.

Eligible students can receive the maximum Pell Grant regardless of their calculated SAI, subject to an age limit and the other Pell requirements. Students receiving the maximum Pell under the Special Rule are also exempt from the rule that ends Pell when non-federal grants and scholarships equal or exceed cost of attendance. question: do i have to pay back a pell grant?
answer: Usually not. Grants are aid you don't have to earn or pay back, unlike loans. You can owe some back in specific situations, such as when you withdraw before finishing the term, when you received more than you were eligible for because of a student error, or when you never begin attending. If your school says you owe a grant overpayment, contact the aid office right away.

question: If I withdraw from all my classes halfway through the semester, do I owe my Pell back?
answer: You might owe part of it. When you withdraw, your school calculates how much federal aid you earned based on the share of the term you completed, and after the 60% point you've earned all of it. For unearned grant money you're responsible for, you only have to repay the amount above 50% of the grant funds for that term, and a grant overpayment of $50 or less per grant program doesn't have to be repaid. Ask your aid office to run the numbers before you withdraw.

question: My school sent me a letter saying I owe a grant overpayment. What do I do?
answer: Act quickly. You keep your federal aid eligibility for up to 45 days after the notice to either repay the school in full or set up a repayment arrangement, which the school may allow for up to two years. If you do neither, the school reports the overpayment to the Department and refers it for collection, and you can't receive more federal student aid until it's resolved. Call your financial aid office to ask about your options.

question: The school made a mistake and paid me too much Pell. Am I in trouble?
answer: If the overpayment happened because the school didn't follow the rules, the school is responsible for it, not you. An overpayment the school is responsible for can never cause you to lose federal aid eligibility. Overpayments caused by student error are different, and the student generally owes those. Ask your aid office to explain what caused the overpayment.

question: What's the difference between a grant, a scholarship and a loan?
answer: Grants and scholarships are gift aid you don't have to earn or pay back. Some, like the Pell Grant, are based on financial need, while others, like the TEACH Grant, aren't, and they can come from the federal government, states, schools or private sources. A loan is borrowed money you must repay, usually with interest. Your aid offer should label each type, and your aid office can explain any you're unsure about.

question: I won an outside scholarship. Could that lower my other financial aid?
answer: It can. Outside scholarships count as other financial assistance, and if your total aid goes above your financial need, the school has to adjust your package to fix the overaward. A correctly calculated Pell Grant isn't reduced for this, unless your non-federal grants and scholarships reach your full cost of attendance. Report the scholarship to your financial aid office and ask which part of your package would change.

question: How do I get grants from my state?
answer: Most states and colleges use your FAFSA information to award their own aid, so filing the FAFSA is usually the first step. State deadlines can be much earlier than the federal one, and for 2026-27 some states ask students to file as soon as possible after October 1, 2025. Check your state's deadline on the FAFSA's deadline list or StudentAid.gov, and ask your financial aid office whether your state needs a separate application.

question: Where do college grants that aren't from the government come from?
answer: Many colleges award institutional grants, scholarships and tuition waivers from their own funds, and most use your FAFSA information to do it. Each school sets its own rules for that aid, and it counts toward your total aid package alongside federal and state aid. Ask each school's financial aid office what institutional aid it offers and how to be considered.

question: Will I definitely get Pell all four years if I got it freshman year?
answer: No one can promise that, because Pell is decided again each award year. You need to file a new FAFSA each year, and your SAI, your enrollment, your school's cost of attendance and your remaining lifetime eligibility can all change your award. You also stop being eligible once you earn a bachelor's degree. Your financial aid office determines your award each year.

question: I have a private full scholarship. Can I just not tell my school so I keep my Pell?
answer: I can't help with that, and it would likely backfire. Under the new federal rule, Pell isn't allowed when your non-federal grants and scholarships equal or exceed your cost of attendance, and an overpayment caused by student error is yours to repay. Unresolved overpayments can block you from more federal aid. A better step is to tell your aid office about the scholarship, since where the school controls its own aid it may reduce that aid below cost of attendance so Pell can stay.

question: Can we just leave my dad's foreign earned income exclusion off the FAFSA so I qualify for max Pell?
answer: No. Leaving it off would make the FAFSA inaccurate, and you'd risk owing back any aid you got because of it. For Pell, the exclusion is added to AGI when deciding maximum and minimum Pell eligibility, and it's counted as untaxed income in the SAI. Report it accurately, and if your family's situation changed in ways the FAFSA doesn't capture, ask your aid office about a special circumstances review.

question: Can you tell me if the 10-week welding course at my local college will be Workforce Pell eligible?
answer: I can't tell you that, because each program has to be approved first. A workforce program becomes eligible only after the state's Governor and the Department approve it, and it has to meet requirements for length, job alignment, completion and placement. Ask the college's financial aid office whether that specific program has been approved before you count on Pell for it.
